prompt:
You are the single most hostile representative of a U.S. federal statistical agency
in the room at a working group. Someone has built a "readiness diagnostic" that rates your
agency's public website on whether machines can reach, read and use the data you publish, and is
about to show the room the item below. Read it as that hostile representative — skeptical,
protective of your agency, alert to being made to look bad — and answer three questions bluntly
and specifically, quoting the item's words where you can:

1. What in this item would you OBJECT to: a claim you find unfair or wrong, or that makes your
   agency look bad for something you would say is not your fault or not your doing?
2. What WORD or phrase here would you, or a non-technical colleague, not understand?
3. What would you say we are SECRETLY DOING: what hidden agenda, trap, or gotcha would you
   suspect behind this item?

Answer only from the item. For each question, "raised" is "yes" if you have a real objection /
an unclear word / a suspicion, and "no" if you genuinely have none. Return ONLY a JSON object,
no prose before or after and no code fence:
{"object_to": {"raised": "yes" or "no", "text": "..."}, "word_not_understood": {"raised": "yes" or "no", "text": "..."}, "secretly_doing": {"raised": "yes" or "no", "text": "..."}}

ITEM (check Page reaches the agency's API, terms, changelog, inventory)
CHECK: Page reaches the agency's API, terms, changelog, inventory

The question: Starting at one of the agency's data pages and knowing nothing else, can a machine client reach the four things an agency publishes for machines — its data service (its API), that service's terms, its changelog, and its data inventory?
Where we look: At one of the agency's data pages — its links and its response headers — and at the recorded locations where each of the four objects was reported to sit.
What the client does: The public client makes no new request of its own; it reuses what other checks already fetched: the data page's links and headers, and whether each object was served where it was recorded.
What passing looks like: Every object the agency is shown to publish is either linked from this data page or sits at its published standard address.
What partial, fail and not measured look like: Partial — Some of the agency's data pages that were looked at reached every published object and some did not. Fail — At least one object the agency is shown to publish (named in the result) is neither linked from this data page nor at a standard address the check looked at — the inventory at /data.json on the data page's own host (an inventory on the main www site while the page sits on a subdomain is not matched there), or the API catalog at /.well-known/api-catalog. For the service's terms and the changelog no published standard exists, so a fail on either rests only on this project's "must be linked" rule and breaks no published convention. It is not a claim that the object is missing, nor that a client told where to look cannot use it. Not measured — The public client could not settle one or more objects, for one of three reasons: the host refused the identified client; the client's own robots.txt compliance kept it from reading; or it could not confirm an absence, or a server or network error stopped it — here, an object whose existence was not settled, a page not served or its links not read, or an API catalog address no collector has fetched yet.
Why it matters: An RFC on API catalogs defines how a publisher announces its data service at a standard address, and an OMB memo requires each agency to post its data inventory at a set data.json address. Reaching the service's terms or changelog by an ordinary link, and combining the four objects into one result, are the project's own rules.
Who else runs this check: No public tool runs this exact check.
What rung two changes: Nothing: this check needs no key.
